sources.publisher: Internet Engineering Task Force / RFC Editor
sources.name: RFC 9000 — QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport
sources.role: QUIC connection, packet, frame, stream, acknowledgment, flow-control and connection-migration contract
verified_facts: QUIC defines a secure, connection-oriented transport carried in UDP datagrams with flow-controlled streams.
QUIC packets carry frames; stream data, acknowledgments and connection control are represented with distinct frame types.
A stream FIN indicates the final size of that QUIC stream, while packet acknowledgments confirm receipt of packet numbers.
semantic_limits: A QUIC packet acknowledgment proves protocol delivery state, not that a complete authoritative source object was reconstructed or validated.
A stream FIN or final size proves the transport stream boundary only and must not be treated as source provenance, a cryptographic file digest or a measurement receipt.
Connection migration, flow control and reliable delivery do not establish exact HMLR parcel geometry, vertical datum, units or terrain accuracy.

sources.publisher: Internet Engineering Task Force / RFC Editor
sources.name: RFC 9001 — Using TLS to Secure QUIC
sources.role: QUIC TLS handshake, encryption-level, key derivation, packet protection and 0-RTT contract
verified_facts: RFC 9001 specifies how TLS is used as the security component of QUIC.
QUIC uses Initial, Handshake, 0-RTT and 1-RTT encryption levels with keys derived through the TLS integration.
0-RTT application data has replay considerations and requires application-specific safeguards.
semantic_limits: Successful packet protection authenticates protected transport content under negotiated keys; it does not prove scientific or cadastral truth.
TLS peer authentication and encryption do not establish source authority for a terrain dataset, exact parcel containment or measurement accuracy.
Accepted 0-RTT data must not create a business row because replay protection and independent execution receipts remain required.

sources.publisher: Internet Engineering Task Force / RFC Editor
sources.name: RFC 9002 — QUIC Loss Detection and Congestion Control
sources.role: acknowledgment, loss detection, probe timeout, RTT estimation and congestion-control contract
verified_facts: QUIC senders use acknowledgments, packet/time thresholds and probe timeouts to detect or recover from packet loss.
Loss detection is maintained per packet-number space, while congestion control and RTT are path properties.
Spurious loss declarations can cause unnecessary retransmission and degraded performance.
semantic_limits: Loss recovery or retransmission proves transport recovery behavior, not unique processing of a source object or absence of duplicated application work.
RTT, congestion window and delivery signals do not validate source bytes, geometry, vertical datum, units or numeric results.
An acknowledgment-driven recovery trace must not be reused as an F-host recovery, dataset-download or terrain-sampling receipt.

sources.publisher: Internet Engineering Task Force / RFC Editor
sources.name: RFC 9114 — HTTP/3
sources.role: HTTP semantics over QUIC, request/control stream, framing, cancellation and connection-error contract
verified_facts: HTTP/3 maps HTTP semantics onto QUIC and uses QUIC streams for requests and control functions.
Request and response messages use HTTP/3 frames, while stream and connection errors have defined effects.
QUIC multiplexing permits independent request streams without TCP-level head-of-line blocking between streams.
semantic_limits: Completion of an HTTP/3 request stream does not prove that a selected distribution is canonical, complete or scientifically correct.
A successful HTTP response and clean stream close do not replace exact object digest, version, provenance and application-level validation.
Multiplexed request success must not create a parcel-height result without source bytes, exact polygon, CRS, EPSG:5701, units, method and execution receipts.
